Let me be clear: no disrespect to the Apple Vision Pro. I genuinely believe the Apple Vision Pro is a solid product. But the iPhone Duo and the Apple Vision Pro are fundamentally different things.

There is a view that the iPhone Duo could face similar issues to the Apple Vision Pro. The reasoning is that its price point and device-specific software could make it a critical darling but a commercial flop. But the two are fundamentally different in nature.

The iPhone Duo won't be held back by the Apple Vision Pro's biggest bottleneck

The biggest issue with this view is that the Apple Vision Pro did not replace any core device. It could function as a portable cinema, or as a window into a better gaming and mixed-reality experience, the immersion of which can genuinely move people.

The Apple Vision Pro does not replace your iPhone or iPad. It is an immersive world that you can tuck into a suitcase. The Apple Vision Pro is primarily a stationary-use device, not a small tablet you can slip into your pocket and carry everywhere.

Then there's the price. The iPhone Duo's starting price of US$1,999 is admittedly not cheap, but it's less shocking than expected. Consumers have always been willing to pay up for a premium smartphone, which precisely reflects just how important phones are in modern life.

The Apple Vision Pro's original US$3,499 price tag was always hard to swallow, and now it's been bumped up to start at US$3,699. That price could almost buy you two iPhone Duos — enough to 'upgrade' to an iPhone Quattro.

Utility, portability, and price combined are what make the biggest difference. Because of these reasons, the Apple Vision Pro could not become a truly mainstream consumer product, and as a result struggled to fully realise its potential.

The iPhone Duo combines iPhone and small iPad in one

The iPhone Duo folds the utility of an iPhone and a small iPad into a pocketable body. It costs roughly the same as buying an iPhone 16 Pro this year and upgrading to an iPhone 17 Pro next year — a spending pattern that isn't all that unreasonable.

Undoubtedly, the iPhone Duo will face a tough battle on the software adaptation front — especially with third-party apps. But Apple has already built a fairly complete narrative around the operating system and native apps, and developers will soon have all the tools they need to build great applications for this versatile foldable screen.

For me, the iPhone Duo's biggest challenge is that it doesn't quite reach the level of a top-tier iPhone just yet. Hopefully, future models can get there.

The most upvoted comment was posted by Radiohedgefund

The hardware itself and the operating system experience remain impressive, but until it actually supports iPad apps (and this issue is frankly less complicated than people make it out to be), it's not really an iPad; and for the same camera setup, £2,000 is simply too expensive. Compared with other foldable rivals, factoring in real-world usability, this device is clearly poor value for money. It's not Apple's best product in any category it belongs to.

These aren't some kind of 'growing pains of the first generation.' Apple should be ahead of Samsung, Honor and Google in every respect, but they chose not to be.

Ideally, of course, you'd want everything an iPhone does best — including a foldable screen — in one device. But at this point, in terms of camera quality and Face ID, the iPhone 18 Pro still wins.

More importantly, for a group of consumers who simply want to try out a new iPhone form factor, those trade-offs don't really matter all that much.

Ultimately, the Apple Vision Pro should envy the 'problems' the iPhone Duo faces.
